newsitem.title: USA: U.S YIELD CURVE -- Greenspan seen flattening curve.
newsitem.headline: U.S YIELD CURVE -- Greenspan seen flattening curve.

text.p: Trying to predict what Alan Greenspan will say at his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony always proves difficult.

But analysts said it is safe to say that the Federal Reserve chief's testimony on Tuesday will change the shape of the U.S. Treasury yield curve -- although not as significantly as in February when Greenspan basically told Congress and the market he was going to raise short-term interest rates.
No matter what he says, curve flattening is expected, with long yields falling most in the event of a market-friendly testimony and short yields rising should he take a more hawkish tone.

"What he is apt to do is play the two-handed economist," said Kevin Logan, senior market economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson North America LLC. "Yet, the (Federal Open Market Committee) has a bias to tighten and he will have to emphasize the upside risk to inflation."
In that case, long bond yields could rise as much as 10 basis points to around 6.65 percent, with short yields rising perhaps by as much as 20 basis points, analysts said.
But, experts said, even a knee-jerk reaction to higher yields would not last long, since there are plenty of buyers out there looking to buy at the lows.
Greenspan's hawkish testimony in late February spooked the market and prompted a rise in interest rates of 20 basis points in a week and about 40 basis over the month of March.
"The market is not offsides like last time so we won't see an extreme reaction," said David Connors, head trader at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
The downside risks are greater than on the upside, traders said, since the market has rallied well past where yields were on February 25, the day before the last Humphrey-Hawkins address.

Still, should Greenspan acknowledge the so-called "new economy" of increased competition, higher productivity and low inflation, the market will "slowly grind higher" and set new highs, said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.

The 30-year bond could fall to 6.40 percent and the 10-year note to 6.125 percent, Dimick said. The two-year note, though, was seen stuck at around 5.86 percent, because the two-year could not fall below 30 to 35 basis points over the 5.50 percent federal funds rate unless there was "serious discussion of easing," he added.
Talk of the next Fed move as a rate cut could surface, some said, should Greenspan mention the structural changes in economies worldwide keeping inflation down.
But Greenspan "has to acknowledge reality (of an economy with low inflation) but in a sober and cautious fashion," Dimick said. "It's not an easy tightrope to walk."
Logan added that the Fed chair would probably want to tilt his remarks in favor of bond bears.
"I don't think he wants to see rates go lower," said Logan. "He doesn't want to stimulate the econmy and does not want to encourage more increases in demand than he expects to occur."
